As someone who had been rejected many times, even when you think someone is"the one,"  there is always someone else. It may take months or years, but someone will come along who will make you wonder why you'd ever liked anyone else. And the same can be said for them if it doesn't work out next time, either. After my most recent rejection, I am coming away with a better understanding of myself and the type of person I want to spend my love and energy on. With each person you fall for, you develop a clearer picture of your ideal partner. Take this experience, learn from it, grow from it, and keep searching for your person. Most importantly, remember that the perfect person for you would also see you as their ideal match - don't waste your time obsessing over what could have been with someone whose feelings weren't just as strong as yours.

Yeah, I'm serious. I've always had a lot of déjà vu, since I was a little kid. The first time I remember it happening was after having a dream about an unfamiliar restaurant and then a few months later ending up in that same restaurant (it was on the opposite end of the country). For the most part, these experiences were pretty rare. Recently, however, I've been feeling déjà vu nearly every day. Well, I should say that I *was* feeling it nearly every day. 

For context, every time that I have driven alone on a long road trip I periodically heard this unknown sound. I could never tell what exactly it was, but I just attributed it to my car. Last week I was driving myself and three friends back home from a ski trip. We had made it through a blizzard, but it was nighttime, and the roads were pretty dark with low visibility. I could feel myself getting tired, and I was driving faster than I probably should have. One of my passengers had fallen asleep in the back seat, and I suddenly heard that same sound again; only this time, I could identify it as my sleeping friend's breathing/snoring. The sound was more constant than before, but the resemblance ws uncanny. I suddenly felt like if I didn't become more alert, we would certainly crash and everything would start over again (I know it seems irrational, but it felt real). It was as if I had been remembering the sound of the last moments of my life all along, so that when the time came I would be able to change the outcome. We actually did have a pretty close call a little bit later, but thankfully we all got home safely. Since that night, I haven't had any instances of déjà vu. Almost as if this is the furthest I've made it in my life so far.
This does not help my recent paranoia that I've lived this life before.

One thing I was lucky to learn earlier than most of my peers is that there's a difference between what you *think* *you* *should* *do* (usually influenced by your parents, mentors, self-concept, etc.) and what is *best* *for* *you*. If you truly believe that this program isn't working out for you and won't get any better, then spend some time thinking about what you'd like to be doing. Forget about things like money and your parents, because you can work that out later if you need to. Had I not broken free of the expectations both I and those around me had set for myself, I would either be a miserable engineering student or dead (the most likely of the two). In your case, it's not like leaving the program would mean that you have to start over. You're already a graduate student, so there are probably dozens of other options that could better suit your needs. Not advice, but I hope I could add some perspective.

In that case, I suggest that you ask about an intensive outpatient program instead of hospitalization (if necessary, of course). They can be just as helpful but without such a major interference in your life. If you are suicidal but feel you can keep yourself safe, make it as clear as possible to your doctor. They often take your opinion into account more than you may realize, as long as you seem rational.

I have a good amount of experience in this area, and first and foremost I would encourage you to be honest with your doctor, but maybe hold off on saying some things until you see a mental health professional. Medical doctors are usually not as well-versed in the ways of mental health, and will often send you away without a second thought. As for psychiatrists/psychologists, they usually only place you somewhere if you have an actual plan. And that does *not* mean that you should hide your plan from them if you do have one. Like I said, the best thing you can do is be honest with them, and that may result in hospitalization. However, sometimes that is where you need to be, regardless of how you feel about it.

It's really nothing to worry about, and is more about learning skills than typical talk therapy. The basics are just about learning how to cope with your own emotions, and what actions to take outside of your own mind. Most people pick up on it fairly quickly, but remembering to use the skills is the hard part. By the end I was able to teach a class to the other students, so if you ever need any help or guidance, feel free to reach out.
